A Japanese translation of a Dutch book on human anatomy, published in 1774 by Sugita Genpaku, Maeno Ryōtaku and their colleagues. It was the first full translation of a Western book in Japan and launched the movement known as Dutch learning, or rangaku.

In 1771 Sugita and Maeno watched the dissection of an executed criminal's body in Edo. They had copies of a Dutch anatomy text, itself translated from a German book by Johann Adam Kulmus. They saw that its drawings matched what they found, while the Chinese medical charts they had learned did not.

They set out to translate it, though they barely knew Dutch and had no dictionary. The work took about three and a half years. They also had to coin Japanese words for body parts; some are still in use.

Western books came in only through the Dutch at Dejima. After this, Japanese scholars studied Western medicine, astronomy and science more widely, preparing the ground for surgeons such as Hanaoka Seishū and, later, the rapid change of modern Japan.
